hints: Compare the dashed line (without inhibitor) and solid line (with inhibitor) in each graph, and focus on the final plateau height at very high substrate concentration.
Remember how a non-competitive inhibitor works: it binds away from the active site so adding more substrate cannot overcome it, which lowers $V_{max}$ but leaves the shape of the curve similar.
walkthrough:
**Recall the normal curve shape**

Think of the dashed curve first. As substrate concentration rises, initial rate rises quickly then levels off to a plateau.

That plateau is the maximum rate:
$$V_{max}$$

**Apply the non-competitive rule**

A non-competitive inhibitor binds to the allosteric site, not the active site. It changes enzyme shape so some enzymes can never work properly.

Adding lots more substrate cannot push it off, so $V_{max}$ is permanently lowered, but the curve still levels off to a plateau.

**Pick the matching graph**

We need a solid line that rises in a similar hyperbolic way but plateaus much lower than the dashed line, even at high substrate concentration.

Only graph D shows this lower plateau, so D is the answer.

options.A: Both curves reach the same $V_{max}$, the solid curve is just delayed. That can be overcome by substrate, so this is competitive inhibition, not non-competitive.
options.B: The solid curve is slower at first but is still climbing toward the same $V_{max}$ at high substrate. That is also the pattern for competitive inhibition.
options.C: The solid line is straight and shows no plateau, so it does not show normal enzyme saturation kinetics at all.
options.D: The solid curve has the same general shape but plateaus at a much lower $V_{max}$. High substrate cannot restore the rate, which is exactly the effect of a non-competitive inhibitor.
